extracted.intended_audience: theologians, political philosophers, jurists, and Christian sovereigns interested in church–state relations
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and argumentation about the rights, limits, and sources of ecclesiastical authority as belonging to Christian civil sovereigns versus the Pope; evaluates scriptural texts and historical precedents used to justify papal claims. Useful for assessing claims of papal supremacy, infallibility, and the scope of ecclesiastical vs civil powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Civill Soveraigne If A Christian, Is Head Of The Church In His Own Dominions
rubrics_metrics.description: From this consolidation of the Right Politique, and Ecclesiastique in Christian Soveraigns, it is evident, they have all manner of Power over their Subjects ... and may make such Laws, as themselves shall judge fittest, for the government of their own Subjects, both as they are the Common-wealth, and as they are the Church: for both State, and Church are the same men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates the sovereign's powers within his dominions: appoint judges and interpreters of canonical scriptures; give strength to excommunications through civil penalties; create and regulate ecclesiastical offices and maintenance (titles, tithes, etc.); delegate religious government (e.g., to the Pope) only as a subordinate civil appointment which the sovereign may revoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kings have power to Baptize, and to Consecrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian Kings have power to Baptize, and to Consecrate both Temples, and Pastors to Gods service ... which most men deny; partly because they use not to do it; and partly because the Administration of Sacraments, and Consecration ... requireth the Imposition of such mens hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the sovereign's office includes authority to perform or authorize sacramental and consecratory acts; practical reasons (time, delegation) explain why kings often do not perform them personally. Historical precedents (Solomon blessing/ consecrating the Temple) support royal competency to consecrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of Hands (designation vs. conferral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands, was a most ancient publique ceremony ... designed, and made certain, the person ... intended in a mans prayer, blessing, sacrifice, consecration ... The use then of this ceremony considered in the Ordination of Pastors, was to design the Person to whom they gave such Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: a public, visual designation of the person or thing intended (less ambiguous to the eye than naming). It served to designate or appoint (not necessarily to convey the Holy Ghost in metaphysical sense). When a sovereign already possesses the power of teaching/ordination by virtue of office or baptism, imposition is a ceremony of designation and may be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of ministerial acts justified by greater charge
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater Charge, (such as is the Government of the Church,) is a dispensation for the lesse. ... A King may also if he please, sit in Judgment ... but the charge that lyeth upon him of Command and Government, constrain him to bee continually at the Helm, and to commit the Ministeriall Offices to others under him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: those who hold a greater public office may and should delegate particular ministerial or teaching duties for practical reasons without loss of legitimacy. Biblical examples (Christ, Paul) who delegated baptism/ministerial acts are given as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration by Kings when sovereignty resides in the King
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Old Testament, though the Priest only had right to Consecrate, during the time that the Soveraignity was in the High Priest; yet it was not so when the Soveraignity was in the King: For we read (1 Kings 8.) That Solomon Blessed the People, Consecrated the Temple ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/legal standard: consecratory rights follow the locus of sovereignty. If political sovereignty is vested in the monarch, acts of consecration may properly be performed by him as part of his combined civil-ecclesiastical role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/identification of Antichrist
rubrics_metrics.description: Antichrist in the proper signification hath two essentiall marks; One, that he denyeth Jesus to be Christ; and another that he professeth himselfe to bee Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical criterion for labeling: both marks must be present to qualify as the proper/definite Antichrist (deny Christ + claim to be Christ). Many persons/officeholders (e.g., popes) who neither deny Jesus nor claim to be Christ do not meet this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texts For The Infallibility Of The Popes Judgement In Points Of Faith (standard of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bellarmines alledged scriptural proofs (Luke 22.31; Matth. 16; John 21, Exod. 28.30) for papal infallibility in matters of faith; these are examined as to whether they grant universal, juridical infallibility to the Pope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exegetical standard: a scriptural text must clearly and unambiguously confer (a) permanent, (b) universal, and (c) jurisdictional infallibility in this world to the person/office claimed. Hobbes rejects Bellarmine's readings: e.g., Luke 22:31 is limited to Peter's personal faith and exhortation to strengthen brethren; Matt.16 concerns the confession of faith, not personal monarchy or juridical infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of certain gospel commissions as teaching, not lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: John 21 'Feed my sheep' contains no more but a Commission of Teaching ... Matth. 16 'Whatsoever yee shall bind on Earth ...' is addressed to all Apostles (Matth. 18.18) and concerns confession and teaching rather than temporal legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hermeneutic rule: passages that command teaching/feeding or binding/loosing are better read as commissions to teach and persuade, not to make temporal laws or claim civil jurisdiction over other sovereigns. Such passages do not by themselves establish universal ecclesiastical legislative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texts For The Same In Point Of Manners (limits on ecclesiastical jurisdiction over manners)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Infallibility of his Judgment concerning Manners, hee bringeth John 16.13 ... but though it were granted, the Pope could not possibly teach any error at all, yet doth not this entitle him to any Jurisdiction in the Dominions of another Prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative conclusion: even if spiritual infallibility (in necessary truths) were accepted, it does not imply jurisdictional authority in the temporal dominions of other princes. Jurisdiction requires additional warrants beyond doctrinal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Law from Counsell
rubrics_metrics.description: Law, is distinguished from Counsell, in this, that the reason of a Law, is taken from the designe, and benefit of him that prescribeth it; but the reason of a Counsell, from the designe, and benefit of him, to whom the Counsell is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: textual style and purpose indicate whether an apostolic or biblical injunction is a law (imperative, concerned with prescriber's ends) or a counsel (advisory, concerned with recipient's benefit). Stylistic markers: 'We command' suggests law; 'We think good' suggests counsel. Acts 15 example (We thought good ...) is counsel, not binding law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of ecclesiastical punishment vs civil punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is he that giveth strength to Excommunications; which but for such Laws and Punishments, as may humble obstinate Libertines, and reduce them to union with the rest of the Church, would bee contemned ... Excommunication, which without the Civill Power is no more but a leaving of their company ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard: excommunication in itself is a spiritual/communal sanction (denouncing, separation) and not equivalent to civil punishments (death, imprisonment, fines). Only the civil sovereign can enforce temporal sanctions; ecclesiastical censures acquire force within a realm only insofar as civil law supports them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral precepts (e.g., Timothy) construed as advice not universal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Timothy 3.2 'A Bishop must be the husband but of one wife, vigilant, sober, &c.' ... I see no reason why to call it a Law, rather than an Advice, seeing Timothy was not a Subject, but a Disciple of St. Paul; nor the flock under the charge of Timothy, his Subjects in the Kingdome, but his Scholars in the Schoole of Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive guideline: many pastoral instructions addressed to named disciples or local pastors are prudential precepts intended as guidance for teaching/discipline within that local or pedagogical context, not universal legislative prescriptions for all Christendom. Use context (addressee, setting) to decide law vs advice.
